---
title: "Fuzzy Generators: From Grades to Outputs"
---

A fuzzy profile describes how values fit. A machine must eventually emit something: a command, a number, or another profile.

The missing piece is an output policy.

This is where the slides' broad idea of a generating structure can connect fuzzy descriptions to an actual sequence.

## 🔰 A profile needs a rule for producing outputs {#sec-sample-fuzzy-generators-a-profile-needs-a-rule-for-producing-outputs}

Suppose a value is described as “about 27” by the triangle on the previous page.

Several procedures are possible:

- Emit its peak, 27.
- Emit an interval selected by a membership threshold.
- Emit its whole profile for another stage to interpret.
- Introduce a probability model and draw a random value.

These procedures preserve different parts of the description. The membership profile alone does not choose among them.

In particular, always emitting the peak is a deterministic generator. Its outputs do not sample the full triangle.

## 🏵 A small fuzzy controller can generate a number {#sec-sample-fuzzy-generators-a-small-fuzzy-controller-can-generate-a-number}

Imagine a demonstration fan controller with two rules:

- When the input fits “cool,” suggest output level 20.
- When the input fits “warm,” suggest output level 80.

These levels are illustrative commands on a scale from zero to 100.

For a particular input, suppose the rule activation grades are $a_{\mathrm{cool}}=0.4$ and $a_{\mathrm{warm}}=0.6$. Choose the weighted output policy

$$
y=
\frac{20a_{\mathrm{cool}}+80a_{\mathrm{warm}}}
     {a_{\mathrm{cool}}+a_{\mathrm{warm}}}
=
56.
$$

Constant rule outputs combined this way form a simple zero-order Sugeno system. The grades express rule activation; the weighted-average output is a chosen inference policy. [MathWorks' description of Sugeno systems](https://www.mathworks.com/help/fuzzy/types-of-fuzzy-inference-systems.html) gives this construction.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-sample-fuzzy-output
%%| fig-cap: "Two graded rules contribute to one command through a declared weighted-average policy."
flowchart TD
    X["Measured input"] --> C["Cool rule: grade 0.4"]
    X --> W["Warm rule: grade 0.6"]
    C --> Y["Weighted output: 56"]
    W --> Y
```

The grades happen to sum to one here. The formula only requires their sum to be positive. Other membership definitions need not create a partition.

If every rule has zero activation, the denominator is zero. The controller needs an explicit fallback or an error state; the formula cannot invent a command.

## ⚙️ Following an input creates a signal {#sec-sample-fuzzy-generators-following-an-input-creates-a-signal}

At each address $t$, evaluate the rules on the input $X[t]$ and apply the output policy:

$$
Y[t]
=
\frac{\sum_j a_j(X[t])\,c_j}
     {\sum_j a_j(X[t])}.
$$

Here $c_j$ is the constant output suggested by rule $j$.

For cool/warm grades $(0.8,0.2)$, $(0.4,0.6)$, and $(0.1,0.9)$, the outputs are

$$
32,\quad56,\quad74.
$$

We have built a numerical signal through fuzzy reasoning. Given the same inputs and rule definitions, this example produces the same outputs.

A controller with memory would add state and update rules, just as our general [Generator](generators.qmd) architecture allows.

## 💡 Randomization is an additional policy {#sec-sample-fuzzy-generators-randomization-is-an-additional-policy}

We could instead choose output 20 with probability $0.4$ and output 80 with probability $0.6$. That random selector has mean 56, but every individual output is either 20 or 80.

The deterministic command 56 and the random selector are different generators.

Likewise, normalizing an integrable membership profile against a chosen measure creates a possible probability model. It does not prove that observations follow that model. Another output policy could use its alpha-cuts or its peak.

This distinction lets us unify the interface without collapsing the meanings: an extended description enters; a declared policy produces the output type.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try the idea {#sec-sample-fuzzy-generators-try-the-idea}

The cool and warm activation grades are both $0.3$. What does the weighted-average controller emit? What would be missing if both grades were zero?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Work it through {#sec-sample-fuzzy-generators-work-it-through}

It emits $(20(0.3)+80(0.3))/0.6=50$. The total activation need not be one. If both grades were zero, no rule would contribute and the weighted average would be undefined; a separately specified fallback would be required.
:::
